judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v Julasiri Bin Akilmara
judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case

judgments.title: CINDY YONG NYUK KHIM v LEE SIANG KORN @ LEE SIANG CHIN & ors

parties.label: RESPONDEN
names: LEE SIANG KORN @ LEE SIANG CHIN

judgments.catchwords: This appeal is, at its heart, about the limits of judicial intervention in the face of parallel but legally distinct proceedings. The Appellant seeks to characterise the dispute as one of timing and forum discipline, urging that the Family Court should speak first on her occupation of the matrimonial home. However, on closer examination, the property in question is not a matrimonial asset, is owned by third parties and has been expressly relinquished in the matrimonial pleadings. The Family Court is not, on the present record, adjudicating any rights over House No. 12A. The alleged overlap is therefore more rhetorical than real. The law on stays of proceedings demands exceptional or unusual circumstances. The Appellant’s personal hardship, while not trivial, does not meet that standard in the face of the Respondents’ clear proprietary rights and the absence of any substantive matrimonial claim to the property. Her delay and tactical conduct further weaken her position. The Sessions Court applied the correct principles, considered the relevant facts and reached a conclusion that is both defensible and consistent with authority. For these reasons, I find that the Sessions Court was not plainly wrong in refusing the stay. The appeal is accordingly dismissed. The order of the Sessions Court dated 27.11.2025 is affirmed. Costs of RM3,500 are awarded to the Respondents, subject to 4% allocator.
